items.stem: Define the term 'relative cell reference'.

items.stem: Eagles Sports Club in Jakarta publishes a report with charts of its sales and customer data. Assess the use of charts rather than tables to present data in the reports of Eagles Sports Club.
items.answer: Points for: trends and comparisons are seen quickly; engaging; suitable for non-specialists. items.stem: Describe the difference between 'bit depth (sample resolution)' and 'transition'.
items.answer: bit depth (sample resolution): The number of bits used to store each sound sample; a greater bit depth records the amplitude more precisely. transition: An effect used when one video clip changes to the next, such as a fade, dissolve or wipe.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: bit depth (sample resolution) correctly described; 1 mark: transition correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: An uncompressed video clip is 1280 × 720 pixels with a colour depth of 16 bits, at 25 frames per second, and lasts 10 seconds. Calculate (a) the size of one frame in MB and (b) the size of the whole clip in GB (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes, 1 GB = 10⁹ bytes).

BlueWave Supermarkets in Karachi is producing podcasts and short videos for its website. (a) Describe two transitions that could be used between video clips. (b) Explain the difference between lossy and lossless compression.
items.answer: (a) Fade; dissolve/cross-fade; wipe; slide; zoom. (b) Lossy permanently removes data (smaller files, lower quality); lossless removes no data (original restored exactly).

items.stem: Define the term 'VLOOKUP'.
items.answer: A function that searches for a value in the first column of a table and returns the value in the same row from a specified column.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A function that searches for a value in the first column of a table and returns the value in the same row from a specified column. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between 'named range' and 'relative cell reference'.
items.answer: named range: A name given to a cell or group of cells, such as VATRate, which can be used in formulae instead of the cell reference and acts like an absolute reference. relative cell reference: A cell reference, such as B2, that changes when the formula is copied to another cell, keeping the same relative position.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: named range correctly described; 1 mark: relative cell reference correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'HLOOKUP' and 'nested IF'.
items.answer: HLOOKUP: A function that searches for a value in the first row of a table and returns the value in the same column from a specified row. nested IF: An IF function placed inside another IF function so that more than two outcomes can be tested.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: HLOOKUP correctly described; 1 mark: nested IF correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Cell D3 contains the formula =B3+C3. It is copied to cell D6. What formula is in D6?
items.markingKey: Relative parts move 0 column(s) and 3 row(s); parts with $ stay fixed: =B6+C6.

items.stem: Jonas is building a spreadsheet for Pioneer Insurance in Hanoi to calculate staff pay and bonuses. Evaluate the use of lookup functions instead of nested IF functions in the spreadsheets of Pioneer Insurance.
items.answer: Points for: lookup tables are easier to read and update; handle many bands; fewer errors. Points against / limitations: nested IF needs no separate table; lookup errors if the table is unsorted or the range is not absolute; #N/A errors need handling. Conclusion: lookups are better for many categories that may change; nested IF suits two or three fixed outcomes.

items.stem: Define the term 'scenario'.
items.answer: A saved set of input values in a model (e.g. best case, worst case) that can be switched between to compare outcomes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A saved set of input values in a model (e.g. best case, worst case) that can be switched between to compare outcomes. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'what-if analysis' and 'scenario'.
items.answer: what-if analysis: Changing one or more input values in a model to see the effect on the results. scenario: A saved set of input values in a model (e.g. best case, worst case) that can be switched between to compare outcomes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: what-if analysis correctly described; 1 mark: scenario correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a business uses a spreadsheet model to answer what-if questions. (b) Explain two limitations of using a computer model to predict weather.
items.answer: (a) It can change inputs such as price or costs and see the effect on profit instantly, without the risk and cost of trying it in reality, helping it plan and make decisions. (b) The model is a simplification, so it may not include all factors; input data may be inaccurate or incomplete; small errors grow over time so long-range forecasts are unreliable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark change inputs/see effect; 1 mark no real-world risk/cost; 1 mark supports decisions. [3] (b) 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark explanation). [4]
